input: agniṣṭhá; compare the feminine and -ikā derivatives explicitly included in Turner

input: aṅká plus an independently identifiable modern u/a nominal formation; an old extension remains reconstructed

The early long aa is compatible with lengthening of an accented short root vowel in an open syllable after extension. Hook to curved sickle is a plausible semantic specialization. It is not evidence that every old final accent simply retracted unchanged.

analysis: Palula angóor, Biori angáar and Gilgit hagáar all accent the inherited medial long vowel early. Guresi aṅgáaru shows the same locus with a retained ending. Old initial short á precedes long ā, so a quantity-sensitive transfer to the later long nucleus predicts the shared innovation. Ashret raising ā to oo postdates this transfer; nasal-cluster simplification and h-prothesis vary separately.

analysis: Palula angeerí continues a final-accented feminine/collective charcoal formation. The final short í and stem ee distinguish it from root-accented angóor ‘fire’. Earlier feminine i/y can explain fronting of the old long a, and the final accent belongs to the derivative rather than to the base's inherited accent.
unresolved: The relative contributions of i-umlaut, vowel shortening and the exact -yā/-iyā formation are not uniquely determined from the citation.

analysis: Palula angúṛu and Strand angʹuṛi retain accent on the old medial vowel while differing in gender/sense (thumb versus finger). input: aṅguṣṭhá with an attested alternate aṅgúṣṭha accent in Turner

unresolved: The origin and date of the u/o formation and dialectal compensation remain to be established. The isolated Sauji record ṭh is a transcription fragment, not a word outcome.

input: feminine ajā́, with possible -akā/-ikā extension, rather than masculine ajá alone

input: átyēti / *átiyēti; the modern citation forms are not all the same paradigm cell
analysis: Palula áača/áače is an accented verbal citation/imperative formation, while Gilgit ač- is an unaccented dictionary stem and achoiki an infinitive. analysis: Palula aáǰ, independently late in Strand, opposes the general early contour of newly lengthened unaspirated short a in a closed monosyllable. Either quantity was restored before the late-lengthening rule or this high-frequency adverb escaped its normal assignment.
unresolved: The source does not decide between an older long input from adyā́, analogical quantity, and lexical preservation of late accent. Retain as a real late-lengthening residual.

analysis: Gilgit on preserves only one short nucleus. Nasal geminate reduction and a-to-o backing are compatible with its segmental history, but the bare short form cannot distinguish inherited fixed accent from a mobile class. Older ōn is a quantity disagreement, not independent mora-accent evidence.

input: apārá ‘near bank’, within the pāra spatial family
analysis: Gilgit -waary and older wāri/wāro are directional bound forms. Loss of the initial syllable and grammaticalization have obscured independent lexical accent; the dictionary stem is unmarked. input: abhrá, with the separately attested abhríya derivative retained as an alternative
analysis: Palula áabru/áabur and Shina áẓo/áj̣u all place accent on the lexical root before the final gender vowel, against final-accented abhrá. input: ardhá ‘half’; the entry also notes comparison with barytone árdha
analysis: Palula áaḍu is early and root-accented before final u. This fits the extended-nominal pattern and subsequent root-a lengthening after rdh reduction. unresolved: The exact relationship of the two old accent variants must remain visible in sensitivity calculations.

input: álpa; alpakám independently attests an extended old adjective
analysis: Kohistani ápa and Guresi/Astori ápo keep root prominence after lp reduction, whereas Degener's Gilgit aápo has late long aa. This is a further test of dialect-specific compensation: an originally short root vowel before a cluster can become late long in Gilgit while remaining short elsewhere. It enlarges the comparison beyond the familiar ‘hot’ example.
unresolved: Gilgit quantity and mora accent should be checked against its paradigm and other sources; the old short a does not itself predict late rather than early compensation.

analysis: Palula -wʹe is a bound locative/directional element with substantial vowel loss and contraction. A short nucleus with prominence cannot distinguish the preservation of old initial accent from accent assigned to the surviving morpheme. Bound use also introduces phrase-level accent interactions.
unresolved: No nominal sound-law count is justified; inspect constructions and morphological scope.

analysis: Palula áašuṇ and Biori áašum are initial-accented with an unaccented second nucleus. They disagree with medial aśáni but agree in accent with the independently attested stone noun áśan. Hail as a stone-like object provides semantic motivation for that alternative, yet the u vowel and final nasal variants need a separate derivation. Shina aĩyĕ́r has later prominence and a different consonantal development.
unresolved: The alternative old noun explains accent only provisionally; do not erase the disagreement by silently substituting it. Shina fragment records n and r are excluded from lexical outcome counts.

analysis: Gilgit aá~ṣo has a late long initial vowel before an unaccented o despite old initial short accent. Together with ‘few’ and ‘hot’, it suggests a class of long vowels created after old consonant clusters. The preserved old root accent locus and changed within-vowel alignment must be coded separately.
unresolved: Nasalization and śr reduction may have produced the compensatory mora; a single modern citation cannot establish its exact timing.

input: áśva, with independently attested aśvaka/aśvikā extensions
analysis: Gilgit ášpo/á~špo keeps initial accent while retaining the śv-derived consonant cluster and a final vowel. Unlike ‘tear’ and ‘few’, it has no compensatory long nucleus in the modern primary sources. Brokskat apš metathesizes the cluster and lacks the final vowel, but its source is unmarked. This is a useful control against lengthening after every old consonant cluster.
unresolved: The relation of the different final-vowel formations to the old simple and extended nouns is not uniquely resolved.

analysis: Biori aṣṭ and short Shina aṣ show loss of the old accented ending with a short surviving stem; Ashret áaṣṭ then fits later unaspirated closed-a lengthening with early accent. Its early contour therefore does not refute inherited final accent. Kalkoti eeṣ requires an independent vowel/umlaut or numeral-paradigm history; its unmarked citation cannot supply tone.
unresolved: The replacement of old ā/au and Kalkoti fronting remain segmental/morphological questions, separate from Ashret mora assignment.

analysis: Ashret aṣṭóoš, Biori aṣṭáaš and Strand asṭʹôš preserve early accent on the contracted teen constituent. The old long accented ā provides an appropriate precursor to early aa and Ashret oo raising. Shina and Sauji retain related contracted numeral shapes. This is an independently compatible model for accentual leveling elsewhere in the teen series.
unresolved: The detailed loss of daśa and the sequence of vowel coalescence are reconstructed; it is not an unextended noun test.

analysis: Gilgit as-, áši and ašíl distribute accent differently across copular stems/cells. The short root form alone is noncontrastive, while the longer preterite formation has a later accent. The old finite present cannot be used as the immediate input for every tense formation.
unresolved: A historical copular paradigm, including suffixal and suppletive material, is required before deriving the later accent.

analysis: Palula aaghaá/Strand âghâʹ has late accent on the surviving final long vowel. Loss of the old final śa and coalescence can preserve right-edge accent; internal k lenition/voicing produces gh. This supports a contraction class rather than the simple CVCá apocope class. Kalkoti äɡa and Kundal ay have more reduced, unmarked forms and need independent cognacy scrutiny.
unresolved: The exact contraction and aspiration chronology remain open; source fragment records k and g are excluded as words.

input: āṇḍá / aṇḍá with independently attested -aka extension
analysis: Palula haṇoó and Guresi haṇoó~ have late accent on the final long ending; Gilgit haneé/haṇeé has the same alignment on a fronted final vowel, while Kohistani haṇó is short. Initial h, loss of old root quantity, medial ḍ reduction and gender/ending replacement show that the modern accented vowel is not a bare reflex of old ā. The shared late ending is consistent with a remodeled egg formation with a historically accented final syllable.
unresolved: Old neuter morphology and the exact route to oo/ee differ by branch; the short Kohistani vowel cannot be treated as an early/late contrast.

input: ātí, with independently recorded āṭi/āḍi variants
analysis: Palula héeṛi and Strand hʹêṛi have early root accent, not the final accent of ātí. A feminine formation with a following i can account for root fronting, but ee has escaped the old early-ee-to-ii change. This independently suggests either a later umlaut layer, later accent retraction, or a later lexical entry into the inherited vowel pattern. Prothetic h and t/ḍ-to-ṛ are additional historical steps.
unresolved: An early-accented old alternative is not supplied by this entry. Retain the accent discrepancy and the chronology of unraised ee.

analysis: Gilgit óẓi ‘belly’ and azaló ‘entrails’ cannot be a single undifferentiated accent outcome: the latter has an extra final formation, the former a root-accented i-stem. The old ntr cluster accounts for a difficult root consonantal history, while the different nominal endings offer a morphological reason for the divergent prominence. Old ā versus short a is independently variable.
unresolved: The exact -i and -aló derivations need to be reconstructed; neither form is clean evidence for final-vowel apocope alone.

analysis: Palula óomu and Biori úumu have early root accent and retain the final gender vowel. This is diagnostic for accent assignment to a long root before extension: the long ā then undergoes Ashret/Biori raising. Copying final accent from āmá would not predict the early raised root. The independently attested āmaka formation makes extension substantially better grounded here than a suffix supplied only from modern u.
unresolved: The accent of the historical extended formation itself is reconstructed; Shina's older unmarked āmŭ confirms shape only.

analysis: Guresi oónu is an infinitive with its own accentual ending; Gilgit áal- is explicitly a perfect stem. The perfective can preserve prominence associated with contracted āyāta, whereas the infinitive cannot be compared directly with the old finite present. The two formations must remain separate in both syllable-locus and mora-outcome tables.
unresolved: The history of l in the perfect and the exact infinitive contraction are not established by the headword links.

input: ārá pronominal family, with independently attested ārā́t and ārḗ

Different deictic categories in Strand and Liljegren caution against pooling their glosses as an unchanged lexical meaning. Final accent is broadly compatible with the old pronominal family's oblique forms.

input: ā́vr̥ta plus the modern u/o adjective formation
analysis: Palula aawíiṛu and Strand awʹiṛo both accent the final root syllable before the gender vowel, despite old initial ā́. The shift cannot be simple attraction to an inherited long vowel because the old second nucleus is vocalic r. An extended-adjective accent rule predicts the locus, while quantity differs between the primary modern sources. Covered or enclosed to narrow/tight is semantically plausible.

analysis: Strand's Palula âṣâʹṛ ‘apricot’ has late prominence on the surviving medial long vowel, compatible with loss of the old final accented syllable and retroflex-stop lenition. The fruit can be named for its season, providing an independent semantic bridge. Gilgit asát ‘month’ retains final short prominence but may reflect an adapted calendar term rather than the identical sound-change chain.
unresolved: Inherited calendar vocabulary versus later learned/contact borrowing must be checked before combining the forms in a historical success rate.

analysis: Palula izraáṇ rainbow and inflected izreeṇí belong to the productive late-accented aa/ee i-declension class. Full Turner1577 connects izrāṇ with indradhanuṣ but explicitly leaves its z/ž development unexplained. Biori niildhráal is a segmentally different lexical alternative with early root accent. The dictionary variant record carries the izreeṇí inflection of izraáṇ; it is not evidence that niildhráal itself has that plural. Its initial niil may invite comparison with the blue adjective, but the remaining component and exact etymology are not established.

input: íṣṭakā, iṣṭikā, and contracted iṣṭā are independently recorded

The loss of medial k and replacement/coalescence of the feminine ending make a reformed nominal stem plausible; an iṣṭā-like reduced base is independently attested. This is not evidence for generic attraction from short í to later ā unless the a-to-u and morphological ending are derived too.

input: īdŕ̥śa / īdr̥śaka; one nearest database section has an empty Original field

analysis: Palula uts and the short Shina cognates have only one short nucleus. They preserve the affricated cluster with branch-specific nasalization or aspiration but cannot reveal early/late long-vowel accent. input: udaká, with daka and udan-related stems independently recorded

input: údbharati, *udbhārayati, and *udbhr̥ta are different old formations

The metathesis of r and preservation of aspiration are relevant to the segmental history, but final íi is a verbal morphological exponent and does not demonstrate a sound shift from old initial ú. analysis: Strand ʹudr has a short surviving nucleus, compatible with loss of old final accented a without an observable mora contrast. Shina ŭẓŭ retains an ending and Sauji uɬ has a distinctive cluster outcome. Their unmarked older citations do not determine accentual class. The otter identification fits the old aquatic-animal meaning.

analysis: Gilgit uni- ‘bring up’ and uníilo ‘nursling’ represent a verbal stem and an extended participial noun. The latter has early long ii on the final stem syllable before lo; its accent belongs to the derivative and cannot be projected back to the prefixed finite verb. Foster-parent compounds add further morphology.

analysis: Strand wʹîway ‘wife’s brother’ is early-accented and radically contracted relative to upapatí. The family link is not sufficient to treat this as evidence for retraction from old final accent.

analysis: Palula bhéša and causative bhešóo have different morphological accents, while Gilgit beéi-/bay- and Kalkoti bišuun represent still other stems/cells. Loss of initial upa- and aspiration displacement must precede comparison of their surviving root vowels. The past -ṭ- base derives from upaviṣṭa, independently distinguishing it from present -š-. The family is informative about a paradigm, not one mechanically retained lexical accent.
unresolved: Test each present, perfective and causative cell separately; the bare Sanskrit present does not supply the accent of all three.

analysis: Gilgit oó~s b- ‘smile’ retains late accent on a long contracted base. Loss of the old final accented vowel can produce right-edge prominence, while loss of internal h and the initial syllable explains why this is not a simple one-vowel apocope case. The light verb is a separate prosodic/morphological word.
unresolved: The coalescence leading to oo and the stage at which h disappeared need checking against the independent smile paradigm.

input: úraṇa; compare úrā and the distinct urial formation
analysis: Gilgit, Guresi and Astori urán all have final short accent against old initial úraṇa. This is a shared substantive residual, not just uncertainty about mora accent: two modern nuclei remain and the wrong one is prominent under simple retention. Gilgit uriín ‘urial’ has additional vowel/derivational history and must be counted separately. A young-animal suffix or old alternate accent is a candidate explanation but is not independently demonstrated.
unresolved: Keep urán as a counterexample to unrestricted syllable-accent retention unless an attested intermediate formation is found.

analysis: Gilgit úu~ṭ has early long accent, compatible with old root prominence through ṣṭr simplification. Since old u was short, the long vowel needs compensation or lexical/contact history; it cannot be cited as retention of an old long vowel. Camel vocabulary also circulates across neighboring Indo-Aryan languages, so the source alone does not date the quantity change.
unresolved: Determine whether nasalization and length entered together and whether the form is inherited or borrowed before using it to define a cluster law.

input: ū́badhya / ū́vadhya, with *ubbadhya also reconstructed in Turner
analysis: Strand wʹâǰ ‘rumen’ has early long prominence compatible with reduction of an initially accented compound-like noun. Semantics are unusually good: undigested stomach contents to the containing stomach chamber. However, old ū may have become the initial glide, leaving a different vowel as the modern nucleus; identity of accent locus cannot be read directly from the long-vowel match.
unresolved: Contraction and the alternate ubbadhya quantity require explicit reconstruction; early modern accent alone does not distinguish the inputs.

analysis: Liljegren húuṇḍ has early long accent, whereas Strand hûʹnḍ- is late. Both show extensive rd(h)v cluster remodeling and aspiration placement. The late reading is compatible with old final-accent apocope if a long root survives; the early reading requires a different quantity chronology or accentual reanalysis. Treat the disagreement as source evidence rather than a dated change.
unresolved: A single preferred accent cannot be selected without speaker/paradigm checks; short huṇḍ and directional suffixes may be relevant.

analysis: Palula iṇc̣ and Gilgit ic̣ are short monosyllables and therefore do not test mora accent. Their i reflects vocalic-r development, and nasalization is secondary. Longer female-bear forms with final accented ī are derivatives of an independently attested feminine formation; they must not be treated as counterexamples to the root-accented masculine noun.
unresolved: Inflection is needed for the simple noun's accent class; early citations disagree over quantity.

analysis: Gilgit ek, Biori ak and Kalkoti äk show shortening/quality change before the modern citation stage. Ashret áak then fits later closed-a lengthening from Biori-like ak. Thus early aa is compatible with the historical accent but cannot be used as unchanged old e length. Turner explicitly discusses the strengthened kk formation, providing a structural reason for earlier shortening.
unresolved: The chronology of emphatic gemination versus borrowing from Sanskrit is unresolved; both produce a different input from bare ḗka.

analysis: Palula akóoš/Biori akáaš and Shina akáai accent the contracted teen constituent, not the original initial é. Unlike áṅgāra, the old accented vowel is itself long, so simple short-to-later-long attraction does not predict this family. Analogy to the teen series and compound restructuring provide a better class-level explanation. Ashret oo raising shows that the new constituent accent predates the relevant vowel shift.
unresolved: The exact contraction and analogy chronology remain reconstructed; do not redefine attraction to include every long-plus-long numeral solely to fit it.

analysis: Gilgit/Guresi óo~ṭo/óo~ṭi and Astori óo~ṭ preserve early accent on the inherited long root vowel. Different gender endings and their loss do not move the root accent. Nasalization and the ṣṭh-to-ṭ outcome are independent segmental changes. This is a strong retention control with both retained and lost final-vowel branches.
unresolved: No accent anomaly in the principal citations; determine gender/sense distinctions before treating lip variants as independent words.

input: ká paradigm, with kaḥ punar and kō’paraḥ explicitly identified as replacement nominatives
analysis: Shina koó/keé and Palula kôʹ have late long prominence, while Kohistani/Astori koé/koí preserve unequal-vowel sequences. Turner independently identifies compound replacements for the simple interrogative; their contraction supplies extra moraic material and a reason not to derive every modern form from bare ká. Gender and number also affect the outcomes.
unresolved: Kundal kō̂ uses its legacy contour convention; source checking is required before assigning a mora label.

analysis: Guresi kácɨ̥ preserves initial accent with a reduced/devoiced ending, fitting root-accent retention. Drasi khiṅ and especially Brokskat caṅ’khoṅ require substantial consonantal or compound history before they can be treated as direct reflexes. The latter's apostrophe marks stress, not a mora contrast. Sauji kačal-ṭɔ̈̄pe is a compound containing related material.
unresolved: Brokskat may contain a borrowed or independently formed second constituent; cognacy must be justified before counting its noninitial stress as an accent shift.

analysis: Short Shina kac̣ and early-long Palula káac̣ fit a common short accented stem after kṣ reduction, followed by Ashret closed-a lengthening. The Palula acute therefore records a newly created mora distinction, while inherited initial accent can be tested through its nominal paradigm. The homonymous armpit family is kept separate.
unresolved: Shina citation forms alone do not establish fixed inflectional accent.

input: káṅkata with independently attested kaṅkatī/kaṅkatikā and other stem variants
analysis: Palula kéengi and Sauji khḗṅgiā have root prominence in an i-containing comb formation, with fronting compatible with feminine umlaut. Gilgit koó~i is late and has lost the medial stop, creating a contraction context absent from Palula. The old entry explicitly contains several suffixes and stem shapes, so a single headword accent does not predict all these formations equally.
unresolved: The inherited versus later origin of Palula ee and the precise Gilgit contraction require independent source/paradigm checks.

input: káḍāra; independently attested karāla and *kaḷāra variants
analysis: Palula karáaṛu and Strand karʹâṛu have early accent on the inherited later long vowel. This is compatible with short-to-long attraction and with final-root-syllable accent in an extended adjective. The projecting-teeth to predator semantic development is plausible. Because both mechanisms predict the same result here, it cannot independently distinguish attraction from extension.

analysis: Palula ǰhām ‘itching’ is unaccented with a long root. Burnt-to-burning/itching sensation is plausible, but the old result adjective and modern state noun are different formations. The comparison with kṣāmá is an alternative, not a supplied accent for jhāma.

analysis: Shina ǰalóiki accents the citation ending and denotes throwing or scattering granular substances. Root shortening and related causative alternatives need a paradigm account.

analysis: Shina tōṅgoṛṓṅ has final long-syllable accent and an expressive repeated nasal/velar pattern. The old clang-plus-kāra formation is onomatopoeic, so sound symbolism and reshaping are independent explanations for its segmental differences. It is not a clean inherited lexical-accent test.

analysis: Shina ṭak boiki ‘be stuck’ contains a short unaccented result element and a be verb. The remain/stop root matches closely. The construction must be separated from the homophonous transitive breaking element under5421 and from whole-infinitive prosody.

analysis: Shina ṭak thoiki ‘break/open a pomegranate’ uses a short impact element with a do verb. Its meaning is distinct from ṭak boiki ‘be stuck’, despite identical nominal-looking material. Expressive root formation and light-verb selection supply independent classes; no accent is marked.

analysis: Shina ṭak ‘button’ is short and unaccented. A stamped disk/coin-to-button transfer is plausible, and the source discusses external monetary vocabulary. The immediate geminate branch differs from ṭaṅka and offers no independently known accent.
unresolved: Read the button etymology and borrowing route and compare garment terminology.

analysis: Shina ṭīku ‘spot’ has long ī before u but no accent. The independently supplied geminate root and related forehead-mark feminine support a derived mark noun, yet the source explicitly calls the tilaka connection obscure. New length cannot be assigned a mora category without marked evidence.

analysis: Shina ṭēru is an unaccented long-root adjective with a direct squinting/crooked meaning match. The old ka extension independently motivates the vowel-final adjective class. Related defective roots have variant consonants and no unique old accent.

analysis: Shina ṭhakur ‘barber’ is unaccented and differs from the old idol/title meaning. Transfer of a social title to an occupational group is possible, but must be documented locally. analysis: Shina ṭhag ‘thief’ is short and unaccented with a close meaning match. Turner explicitly doubts straightforward links to sthagayati and other proposed Sanskrit sources. The expressive or contact root is usable as a modern lexical class but has no secure old accent to test.

analysis: Sawi ḍal ‘big, thick’ is a short unaccented adjective derived plausibly from lump or bulk. The old family is explicitly expressive with several vowel and consonant variants. It cannot supply a unique historical accent or length prediction.

analysis: Sawi ḍik ‘drive off’ is a bare unaccented verb linked to a stick/line noun. Driving with a stick provides a possible denominal route, but the source must establish it. The short root and expressive input provide no long-mora evidence.

analysis: Shina ḍukiní ‘fighting’ accents final short i after an extended nominal formation. The fist-blow root directly supports combat semantics, while the ini suffix independently distinguishes this from a free monosyllabic impact term. Old accent is unknown.

analysis: Palula and Shina ḍup is a short unaccented sinking/plunged-in element. Turner explicitly treats the root as a metathesized counterpart of buḍyati, so that relationship is an independent historical proposal. Result element, simple verb and causative must be kept apart.

analysis: Shina ḍūṅo ‘small earthen vessel’ has long ū before o without accent. The trough/boat-to-container semantic family is plausible and independently reconstructed, but the source considers non-Indo-Aryan origin and influence on drṓṇa. That accented word cannot be adopted as the input automatically.
unresolved: Read the vessel type and borrowing/contamination argument and compare nominal inflection.

analysis: Palula ḍīu ‘part, portion’ is unaccented and contracted, likely requiring the long-e b-bearing branch rather than the broad dhappa headword. Lump-to-portion is semantically close, but the large expressive family does not establish a unique old accent or vowel history.

unresolved: Verify the actual shield gloss and quantity and local contact history.

analysis: Chilas ḍūs ‘hole’ and dum-dus/dūm-dūs ‘smokehole’ are unaccented, with quantity and compound variants. Push-to-pierced-hole is a possible result-noun derivation, but the old expressive root alone is incomplete. The smoke component's vowel must not be assigned to the hole root.

analysis: Sawi ḍuiṅgya ‘elbow, ankle bone’ is an unaccented extended noun with a complex vowel sequence. The old projecting-body-part meaning fits both joints, but the ya ending and initial vowel history require an independent derivation. It is not an unextended monosyllable.
unresolved: Read the anatomical identification and ya formation and interpret the diphthong/hiatus convention.

analysis: Shina tagā́ ‘mud’ accents final long ā, while the old reconstructed root is unaccented. Turner explicitly compares a Burushaski mud form, making contact a concrete possibility. The final-vowel nominal formation and donor direction must be established independently of the observed accent.
unresolved: Read the Burushaski comparison and local mud noun inflection and borrowing evidence.

analysis: Kalkoti tee ‘and’ is an unmarked contracted conjunction linked to an old concessive expression. Even-so to connective use is a plausible grammaticalization, but the exact contraction and competing deictic-particle origins need testing. The constituent accents táthā and ápi do not establish the whole input's prosody.
unresolved: Read the connective's usage, explicit tone evidence and source etymology and compare neighboring conjunctions.

analysis: Shina talúṇu has short prominence in the final root syllable before u, while tanulo is an unmarked cloth adjective. The same talúṇu also appears under táruṇa5712, so metathesis and competing thin/young inputs must be evaluated independently. Parent tanú does not establish tanula's accent.

analysis: Shina tan ‘body’ is short and unaccented; tan-nano ‘naked’ is a body-plus-naked compound. The old final accent is known, but shortening and final-vowel loss remove a long-mora contrast. Compound prosody must not be counted as the free body's outcome.
unresolved: Find marked body paradigms and parse the naked compound and contact history.

analysis: Kundal tā̃d/tand differs in vowel length and nasalization notation, with no explicit accent. The old barytone and nt cluster are independently known, but the source variants may reflect real quantity or alternative transcriptions. They cannot be collapsed into a single mora reading.

analysis: Palula trānd ‘web, weaving’ is unaccented and has metathesis, long ā and final cluster reordering. The old barytone is known, making it a potential historical control, but it is distinct from the wasp compound traambú and from tantra-vāya derivatives in adjacent families.

analysis: Kundal tapgal ‘hot’ contains a recognizable result/adjectival ending and an unaccented tap root. The database's old heat noun tapyatí is not itself a verbal present, despite its shape. A tap verb or participial formation may be the actual immediate input and must be established independently.
unresolved: Read the Kundal gal morphology and source etymology and distinguish heat noun from heated participle.

analysis: Shina taróiki accents the citation ending, while the old simple present is root-accented. The matching crossing sense is strong, but the modern infinitive ending is not evidence that every finite cell shifted accent. The transitive counterpart under5796 is a separate formation.

analysis: Shina talúṇu ‘thin’ has short final-root prominence before u, unlike the old headword's initial accent. Modern adjective remodeling is a possible explanation only after the exact input is settled.

analysis: Shina c̣akiní ‘taking care of’ accents final short i in an extended action noun. The old action noun is unaccented and not identical to the modern suffixal formation.

unresolved: Read the Kalkoti tense label and contact history and compare run/jump paradigms.

analysis: Sawi tal/thal ‘throw’ differs in aspiration and is unaccented. The old place/fix result sense offers a plausible put-to-throw path, but simple and causative formations differ independently. The aspiration variant needs source verification before a historical root is selected.
unresolved: Compare the two transcriptions and the throw paradigm and source semantic argument.

analysis: Shina aiyo ‘such’ is unaccented; starred *taiyo is a reconstructed intermediate rather than an attested variant. Loss of initial t and contraction of the appearance component need independent evidence. The old middle-root accent is known but cannot be tested from the bare form.
unresolved: Read the deictic paradigm and exclude the starred intermediate from modern attestation counts.

analysis: Palula tāmba and Kohistani tāmbā are unaccented copper forms with mr-to-mb development. The old oxytone is known, but the material term's regional transmission and final-vowel morphology require checking. Neither modern long vowel alone supplies an accent outcome.

analysis: Shina taróiki ‘take across’ and tarižóiki ‘cross’ differ in valency and passive/y material, though both accent the citation ending. The old causative is independently accented; modern stem shortening and the intransitive counterpart under5702 must be compared by cell.

unresolved: Verify Pales versus Jijel source cells, quantity and ka formation and compare modern palate paradigms.

analysis: Shina tuloiki ‘prepare a plough, saddle a horse, load a gun’ is unaccented and extends beyond lift/weigh. Equipping or making ready offers a semantic route, but the source must substantiate it. The verb's citation ending cannot establish old or modern root accent.

analysis: Shina tul ‘weight, strength’ is a short unaccented noun after loss of final ā. The old final accent and weighing sense are independently known; strength is a plausible extension from weight or force. A long-mora opposition is absent from the citation.
unresolved: Read weight versus strength usage and seek marked inflected forms.

analysis: Shina túṭu has initial short-root accent before u after ṣṭ reduction. The old result adjective is unaccented here, but its morphological class is independently clear. It supplies a short-cluster control rather than evidence for either inherited barytonesis or a long-vowel law.

analysis: Guresi c̣ayōnu and Kohistani c̣ōnu/c̣užōnu are unaccented cold/shiver verbs with different y/ž and vowel formations. Trembling-to-cold is a direct physiological bridge. The old family has several independently different presents, so one headword accent cannot cover every modern cell.

analysis: Gilgit c̣ā, Kohistani c̣haũ and Guresi c̣avū̃ are unaccented cold-state forms after different contractions. A shivering link to fear is plausible from related verbs, but grammatical noun/adjective status and final-vowel morphology need checking. The old noun is unaccented.

analysis: Shina dádu ‘has been burnt’ has initial short-root accent before u after cluster reduction. The modern source must establish the actual meaning and cell before these are treated as homophones or duplicate analyses.
